notes: Scope limited to major battles of the Gallic Wars (58-50 BC) and the Civil War (49-45 BC); earlier propraetorship in Hispania Ulterior (61 BC) excluded for lack of battle-level data.

Scope limited to major set-piece battles/sieges of the Persian campaign (334-326 BC) with quantifiable troop/casualty estimates. Excludes the 335 BC Balkan campaign (destruction of Thebes), the Battle of the Persian Gate (330 BC, widely described by ancient and modern sources alike as costly but with no surviving casualty figure at all, not even a disputed one), most of the Sogdian guerrilla campaign beyond Cyropolis/Jaxartes, the Mallian campaign (326-325 BC, no quantifiable casualty figures found despite being well attested qualitatively), and the return march and death (323 BC). Alexander is universally regarded as undefeated in pitched battle -- every row here is a Win, unlike the mixed records of other generals in this dataset.

Scope limited to major battles/sieges personally commanded (or personally supreme-commanded) by Genghis Khan with quantifiable troop-strength estimates, spanning the 1204 unification wars through the final 1226 Western Xia campaign. Excludes the Battle of the Thirteen Sides/Koyiten (1201) and the Battle of Khalakhaljid Sands (1203, Genghis's one major personal defeat) for lack of any troop or casualty figures in available sources; excludes the 1213-1215 Siege of Zhongdu for the same reason despite Genghis's personal command throughout. Also excludes battles led by subordinates in Genghis's name rather than under his personal or supreme direction: the 1208 Battle of the Irtysh River (Jochi), the Battle of Parwan (1221, Shigi Qutuqu, a Mongol defeat), and the 1221 sieges of Merv, Nishapur, and Gurganj (Tolui/Jochi/Ogedei/Chagatai). A systemic sourcing gap distinct from the ancient generals in this dataset: unlike Roman/Greek historiography, which nearly always states some own-side casualty figure (however self-serving), Mongol-era primary sources (the Secret History of the Mongols, Persian chronicles like Juvaini and Rashid al-Din, the Chinese Yuan Shi) and the modern historiography built on them almost never quantify Mongol losses, only the (often much larger) toll inflicted on the enemy. Every own_casualties figure in this general's rows is therefore an order-of-magnitude estimate inferred from qualitative source language ('light', 'minimal') or a single specific anecdote (the Zhongxing flood), not a source-attested count -- flagged per-row and noted here as the softest-sourced field across this entire dataset, ancient or medieval.
